blocks.head: Council Votes 7–2 to Keep the Harbor Light Burning
blocks.sub: Town will lease the tower from the Coast Guard for a dollar a year and pay the keeper out of the mooring fund

blocks.caption: Still standing. The Harrow Bay light at dusk on Sunday, photographed from the breakwater. The tower has been dark on three nights since August, when the automatic timer failed.

body: The selectmen voted seven to two on Sunday evening to take over the harbor light, ending eleven months of hearings that filled the Grange hall past its posted capacity on four separate nights.

Under the agreement read aloud by town counsel, the Coast Guard will lease the tower and the quarter acre beneath it to the town for one dollar a year, for ninety-nine years. The town accepts the roof, the stair, the lamp room and the cistern, and the cost of keeping all four from falling into the water.
“We are not buying a monument,” said Selectman Rufus Pell, who moved the vote. “We are buying a job of work that somebody has to do, and it may as well be us.”

The keeper's wage — eleven thousand dollars a year, plus the apartment on the second landing — will come out of the mooring fund, which held $63,400 at the close of the fiscal year. Harbormaster Elvie Shand said the fund can carry the wage for six years without a rate increase, and longer if the summer moorings fill.

Voting against were Selectmen Dorcas Winn and Able Fry, both of whom argued the figure leaves nothing for the stair. An engineer's report filed in March put the cost of replacing the cast-iron treads at $214,000 and recommended the work be done inside four years.
“I have no quarrel with the light,” Mrs. Winn said. “I have a quarrel with a budget that pretends the stair will wait for us.”

blocks.head: Ferry Fare Goes to $3.25 as Fuel Bill Climbs
body: The island run will cost a quarter more from November 1, the first increase in four years. The ferry district blamed diesel, which it bought at $4.18 a gallon in September against $3.02 a year ago.
Commuter books of forty rides stay at the old price until the end of the month. Scholars, and anyone over seventy, continue to ride free on the 6:50 and the 4:20.
The district also warned that the Tuesday freight run may be cut to fortnightly if the Nellie Rand's gearbox is not repaired before the weather turns.

blocks.head: Roof Bond Goes to Voters in November
body: The district will ask for $1.9 million to replace the flat roof over the gymnasium, which has been patched eleven times since 2019. Superintendent Nadia Okonjo said the January thaw is the deadline that matters.

blocks.head: Dragger Aground on Siskin Ledge; No Injuries
body: The 48-foot Pearl Agnes went on the ledge in Friday's fog and came off on the flood with no water in her. The owner said the radar had been down since Thursday. The Coast Guard has asked for a written report.

blocks.small: Storm windows cut to size while you wait. Open 7 to 5, Saturdays to noon. We still deliver.

blocks.head: Mind the Stairs
body: Sunday's vote was the easy half. A dollar a year is not a price, it is a handshake, and handshakes do not replace cast iron. The town now owns a tower that the sea has been working on for a hundred and thirty-eight years, and the sea does not take November off.

We supported the lease and we support it still. The light is not decoration. Two hundred and forty working boats clear this harbor in a season, and a good number of their skippers will tell you, without being asked twice, which flash they look for when the fog shuts in off Siskin. A town that lets that go dark to save eleven thousand dollars has misread its own ledger.

But Selectman Winn is right about the stair, and the applause she did not get on Sunday does not make her wrong. The engineer's figure is $214,000 and it will not get smaller. The mooring fund cannot carry both the keeper and the treads, and pretending otherwise at town meeting in March will cost us the credibility we will need when we ask.

So begin now. Put the stair on the warrant as its own article, with its own number, so that nobody can vote for the light and against the climb. Ask the state for the historic match, which Rockland got two years ago for less cause. Let the Harbor Light Association raise its share in public, with a thermometer on the board outside the post office, because this town gives when it can see the line move.

And hire a keeper who can be trusted with a logbook. Miss Quill's father wrote down the weather every night for thirty-one years in a hand you can still read. That is the standard. It is not a high one, and it is the whole job.

blocks.text: “Thirteen men came off that ledge because somebody climbed those stairs.”
blocks.who: — Hester Quill, at the Grange hall, Sunday

blocks.head: Light: lease runs ninety-nine years
body: Forty-one residents spoke before the vote, and the hall ran out of chairs at a quarter past seven. The longest applause followed Hester Quill, eighty-eight, who keeps the logbook her father kept. “Mind the stairs,” she said.
The lamp will be relit at sundown on Friday. The town has advertised the keeper's post, and applications close on the twentieth.

The lease was drafted by the district office in Boston and differs in one respect from the agreement the town rejected in February: the Coast Guard retains the lamp itself, as an aid to navigation, and will maintain the optic and the charted characteristic.

That leaves the town responsible for the structure, the grounds, the cistern and the fence, and liable for anyone who climbs the stair with permission. Counsel advised the town carry a million in additional coverage, at an estimated $2,300 a year, and the selectmen agreed without objection.

Applications for keeper close on October 20. The post requires residence in the tower from November through March, a current first-aid certificate, and the ability to climb eighty-four steps carrying a load.

items.head: The fund was for moorings
body: Sir — I have paid a mooring fee for twenty-six years and I was told every one of those years that the money was for the floats, the chain and the dredging. On Sunday it became a payroll. If the town wants a keeper, let the town vote a keeper's line in the budget where I can see it, and leave the fishermen's money where it was put.

items.head: My grandfather's hand
body: Sir — The logbook Miss Quill read from on Sunday sat in our kitchen for eleven years after the station closed, because nobody at the state would take it. Whatever the stair costs, do not let that happen to the next thirty years of weather. Put the new keeper's book in the library when it is filled.

items.head: Count the cars
body: Sir — Before the ferry district raises my fare again I would like somebody to count the cars that cross on the 4:20 with one person in them. I counted on Thursday. There were nineteen. The boat is not expensive. We are.

items.head: A quieter blast, please
body: Sir — Whatever is decided about the lamp, the foghorn now sounds every twenty-eight seconds and my house is four hundred feet from it. I supported the lease. I would support it more warmly at forty seconds.
A story on Friday gave the length of the Pearl Agnes as 58 feet. She is 48 feet. The Guble regrets the error.
A caption on September 29 identified the boat at the town float as the Mary Bight. It was the Two Brothers.

blocks.head: Eighty-four Steps, and What's at the Top
body: I climbed the tower on Saturday with the harbormaster, who has a key and the patience of a man who has given this tour before. Eighty-four steps, as advertised. The eleventh and the forty-second ring wrong under a boot, and you learn to hear it by the second landing.

The lamp room smells of hot dust and old brass. There is a chair up there with a cushion somebody's mother made, and a shelf of paperbacks swollen fat with damp, and a coffee ring on the sill that nobody has had the heart to wipe.

What surprised me was the quiet. You expect wind. What you get, with the door shut, is the sound of your own breathing and, every twenty-eight seconds, the horn going off below you like a door slamming in another house.

Whoever takes the post will spend the winter in that quiet for eleven thousand dollars. I hope we get fifty applications. I expect we will get nine, and that four of them will be from away, and that the one we hire will be from here and will not mention the money at all.
Published every morning except Sunday at 14 Wharf Street, Harrow Bay
Letters: 150 words, signed, with a street. Telephone 207·555·0188. Carrier delivery $4.75 the week.

blocks.head: Harbor Light Take It 3–1 on a Field Like Soup

body: Two goals in four minutes either side of the half settled a final that the rain had been trying to settle all afternoon. Teodora Vasiliev got both of them, the second off a corner that nobody cleared because nobody could stand up.

Ashcroft pulled one back on the hour through Hollis Mbeki and then spent twenty minutes camped on the edge of the box without once getting the ball down. Niamh O'Driscoll's save at the near post in the eighty-first was the best thing on the field.
It is the first county title for Harbor Light since 2011 and the first under coach Benedikt Thorvaldsen, who said afterward that he had told them at the half to stop passing and start kicking.

items.name: QUILL, Alvah T.
items.body: 91, of Light Road, on October 2 at home. Coast Guard, 1954–58. Kept the Harrow Bay station logbook with his sister Hester for nineteen years. Survived by Hester, four nieces, and the dory he built in 1971. Services Thursday at eleven, First Parish. The family asks for no flowers and a dollar to the Light Association.

blocks.head: Who Pays When the Float Breaks Loose?
body: Q. The town float came adrift in the September blow and fetched up against my skiff. Is the town good for the gelcoat? — Dented, Cove Road

A. The town insures the float, not what it hits, unless the chain was the town's fault. Ours parted at a shackle we replaced in May, so file a claim at the office with two photographs and the yard's estimate. Do it before the thirtieth. After that I'm on the water and the paperwork waits for me.
